title: When you fail practice
tomorrow: why would a man lie face down in the mud for a Buddha?

lines: A FIB, AND TWO SUNDAYS GONE.
WHY PRAISE THE ONE WHO SLIPPED?
cards: Somewhere there's an app streak showing a sad little zero where a long run used to be. It's tempting to quit right there: the record's broken, so why bother? Mai's version is worse.
She skipped two Sundays of the kids' class and told Chị Hạnh she was sick when she wasn't. Now going back feels impossible. Here's an odd line for her.

The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, says: "He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds." Why praise the one who slipped?

teach.b: Look at the picture. The moon behind clouds isn't gone. It never stopped shining; it was covered.
When the clouds move, it's simply there again, and the night is brighter for it. The verse doesn't pretend the reckless time never happened. It says what comes after counts.
And Buddhist practice builds coming back into its routines.

teach.h: A MONK CONFESSES, AND IS CLEAN.
teach.b: In the Vinaya, a monk who breaks a minor rule confesses it to another monk, and then he's clean again. On the observance day, the uposatha, the monks gather to recite their rules together.
In Theravada temples, lay people often ask for the precepts again at the start of a gathering, taking them up fresh, as if expecting that everyone will need to.
That's the teaching: a broken precept isn't the end of the path.

teach.h: NAME IT, SET IT RIGHT, RETURN.
teach.b: It's a place to return from. Not by pretending, and not by punishing yourself for months. By naming it plainly, setting it right where you can, and taking the precept up again.
For Mai, that means one honest sentence to Chị Hạnh, and a Sunday back with the kids.

how: Monks confess minor offenses to one another and recite their rules together on uposatha days; in Theravada temples lay people often request the precepts again at the start of a gathering, taking them up anew.

games.q: what does “when you fail practice” mean?
o: a teacher sending a student away for good
breaking a precept or drifting away from practice
failing the test to become a Buddhist monk

games.q: the moon and the clouds — tap the pairs.
p: clean again after a minor fault
a fresh start at a temple gathering

s: once you break a precept, you're off the Buddhist path
the Vinaya builds in confession, and lay people take the precepts up again and again.
Dhammapada 172 compares someone who turns around to the moon freed from clouds
the reckless past doesn't cancel the brightness after.
coming back means punishing yourself first, for as long as you were gone
name it, set it right where you can, and take the precept up again.

games.q: you promised your little brother you'd stop yelling at him, then yelled twice this week. what fits today's verse?
o: drop the promise; clearly you can't keep it.
name it, apologize, and take the promise up again today.
wait a month to prove you've changed, then try again.
games.why: the one who was reckless and turned around brightens the world like the moon from clouds. coming back, honestly, is the practice.

practice: Bring to mind one thing you've let slide: a promise, a habit, a precept. Don't argue with yourself about it. In one quiet sentence, out loud or under your breath, name it plainly and say you're taking it up again.
Then sit, and let the clouds move as they will.

wordCard.voice: When you fail practice: a broken precept, a missed month. The moon behind the clouds was never gone.

orig.note: Pali: the observance day, when monks recite their rules together and lay people renew the precepts.

carryVoice: Come back: the moon shines again the moment the clouds move off. Glad you're here.

sources.q: He who formerly was reckless and afterwards became sober, brightens up this world, like the moon when freed from clouds.

sources.ref: Vinaya Pitaka: confession of offenses, and Mahavagga II (Uposathakkhandhaka: the observance day and recitation of the Patimokkha)
